toolchain_choice.title: Screen capture toolchain
toolchain_choice.why: Portal-first capture keeps the planning model honest across mixed Wayland desktops while still leaving room for wlroots-native tools when they exist.
toolchain_choice.risks: Portal routing and consent are desktop-shaped, so screenshot/capture advice must stay capability-aware.

install_commands.apt: sudo apt-get install -y xdg-desktop-portal grim slurp
install_commands.dnf: sudo dnf install -y xdg-desktop-portal grim slurp
install_commands.zypper: sudo zypper install -y xdg-desktop-portal grim slurp

toolchain_choice.title: Trigger / hotkey toolchain
toolchain_choice.why: Triggers on Wayland should be split between portal-aware global shortcuts, compositor-native binds, and launcher surfaces instead of assumed to be one generic backend feature.
toolchain_choice.risks: Global shortcut availability is still desktop/version dependent, so keep a launcher path available for conservative targets.

toolchain_choice.title: Window/context toolchain
toolchain_choice.why: Window-aware Wayland projects should treat context lookup as a desktop-specific metadata bridge rather than a universal primitive.
toolchain_choice.risks: Desktop-specific metadata can be excellent locally but should stay behind a contract so projects remain portable.

stack_profiles.title: Selector-driven runner profile
stack_profiles.summary: Best for visual workflows that need explicit assets, retries, and diagnostics. The runner stays central, but only after selectors become a maintained subsystem.
stack_profiles.ownership_split: Keep the complex timing, retries, and evidence collection inside VHK instead of pushing that state into compositor helpers.
stack_profiles.why_linux_native: Visual automation on Linux needs inspectable assets and debug evidence because raw desktop APIs stay uneven across sessions.
stack_profiles.execution_surface: selector assets + bounded capture + report loop
usage_hints: Selector assets and review traces are part of the runtime contract for visual macros.

stack_profiles.title: Remap-integrated profile
stack_profiles.summary: Best when the project needs ergonomic layers, tap-hold logic, or fast always-on key dispatch. Use VHK as the macro/orchestration brain and let a dedicated remapper own the interception layer.
stack_profiles.ownership_split: Keep interception and tap-hold logic in dedicated remappers, but keep macro meaning in VHK.
stack_profiles.why_linux_native: evdev/uinput-class tools win by staying narrow and fast; VHK should consume them, not become them.

runtime_seams.title: Runner core
runtime_seams.responsibility: Own sequencing, waits, retries, variables, prompt forms, diagnostics, and macro meaning.
runtime_seams.why_split: AHK-class usefulness comes from a strong runtime contract, not from pushing every capability into the trigger layer.
contracts: macro semantics stay stable across desktop backends
logging/diagnostics are available regardless of trigger surface

runtime_seams.title: Trigger and dispatch surface
runtime_seams.responsibility: Wake the right macro quickly through hotstrings, launcher entries, WM binds, remapper keys, or event emitters.
runtime_seams.why_split: Linux trigger ownership is desktop-shaped; treating it as a thin seam keeps the runtime portable.
contracts: the trigger surface launches or emits into VHK without re-implementing macro logic
notes: Always-on hotkeys should stay reviewable because ownership shifts across X11, portals, compositors, and remappers.

runtime_seams.title: Selector and evidence pack
runtime_seams.responsibility: Keep needles, OCR regions, previews, baselines, and review traces inspectable so visual macros are evidence-driven.
runtime_seams.why_split: Visual automation becomes expensive quickly; shipping the evidence pack keeps cleanup and portability review grounded.
contracts: every visual flow can point to at least one selector asset or preview artifact
report/preview commands stay usable on target desktops
notes: Do not hide visual fragility behind extra sleeps.

ecosystem_lessons.title: Keep the runtime rich, not the trigger layer
ecosystem_lessons.summary: AHK feels powerful because waits, retries, variables, and diagnostics stay close to the runtime contract instead of being scattered across hotkey plumbing.
ecosystem_lessons.product_implication: VHK should keep sequencing and diagnostic state in the runner core even when triggers/export surfaces are split out.

ecosystem_lessons.title: Treat recorder output as draft material
ecosystem_lessons.summary: Pulover-style workflows stay productive because recording, inspection, visual steps, and cleanup are part of one authoring loop.
ecosystem_lessons.product_implication: VHK should keep selector assets, optimize/scaffold/report loops, and visual review artifacts first-class instead of pretending raw recordings are shippable.

ecosystem_lessons.title: Keep privileged remappers thin
ecosystem_lessons.summary: Low-level remappers win by staying narrow: intercept keys quickly, then hand richer logic off elsewhere.
ecosystem_lessons.product_implication: VHK should export configs for fast trigger ownership, but keep prompts, variables, selectors, and diagnostics in user-space runtime layers.

ecosystem_lessons.title: Be explicit about desktop/session scope
ecosystem_lessons.summary: Adjacent Linux automation tools still have to be blunt about where they work well and where they do not.
ecosystem_lessons.product_implication: VHK support claims, setup docs, and release gates should name reference lanes and caveated lanes instead of implying generic Linux parity.

ecosystem_lessons.title: App-scoped behavior needs context bridges
ecosystem_lessons.summary: Per-app remapping and context-sensitive behavior on Linux often depends on compositor- or desktop-specific active-window context bridges.
ecosystem_lessons.product_implication: VHK should treat app/window scoping as a capability with backend-specific implementations and review steps, not as one global checkbox.
